title: The Little Book of Common Sense Investing

facts.claim: Bogle's exhibit on costs: $10,000 invested in the stock market for 50 years grows to about $469,000. The same $10,000 in a fund that returns 5.5% a year after costs grows to about $145,400, a shortfall of $323,600.
facts.source: Acquirer's Multiple post quoting the book; arithmetic checked (8% vs 5.5% compounding)

facts.claim: Cost erosion along the way: after year 1 about $10,800 vs $10,550 (about 2% lost); year 10 about $21,600 vs $17,100 (21% lost); year 30 about $100,600 vs $49,800 (50% lost); at the end costs took nearly 70% of what the market would have accumulated.
Bogle: the investor supplied 100% of the capital and bore 100% of the risk but earned only 31% of the market's return.

Bogle's lines: 'The miracle of compounding returns is overwhelmed by the tyranny of compounding costs.' 'Where returns are concerned, time is your friend. But where costs are concerned, time is your enemy.'

Bogle says picking a mutual fund that will beat the market over the long run is, in Cervantes' observation, like looking for a needle in a haystack; his corollary: 'Don't look for the needle in the haystack. Just buy the haystack!' A broad index fund owns the whole market (the haystack).

Bogle's arithmetic: gross return minus costs equals net return; investors as a group earn the market's return before costs and less after them. The theme recurs through the book ('the relentless rules of humble arithmetic').

Chapter 'The Grand Illusion': over the 25 years 1980-2005 the S&P 500 averaged 12.5% a year while the average fund investor earned 7.3%. Costs explain only part of the gap; the main cause is investor behaviour, especially timing and fund selection.
Investors tend to buy funds after they have performed well and sell after they have performed poorly.
The book's subtitle: 'The Only Way to Guarantee Your Fair Share of Stock Market Returns'.
Bogle added to his exhibit a real stretch: in the 1980s and 1990s stocks averaged 17.5% a year and the average fund 15%.
facts.source: Acquirer's Multiple post quoting the book

facts.claim: Illustration computed by the writer, not stated by Bogle: taken as steady annual rates over 25 years, $10,000 at 12.5% grows to about $190,000 and at 7.3% to about $58,000.
A separate survey (Dalbar, 20 years ending Dec. 31, 2010) found stock fund investors earned 3.83% a year against 9.14% for the S&P 500; reported in the same article as Bogle's figures.

rejected.claim: Two investors, $10,000 a year for 40 years, 7% market return, 2% vs 0.05% fee, ending at $1.1M vs $2.1M.
rejected.reason: Not Bogle's exhibit; the book's exhibit is $10,000 over 50 years ($469,000 vs about $145,400).

rejected.claim: 'Cost paradox' term and active managers do more analysis and trading.
rejected.reason: Term not found in the book.

rejected.claim: S&P SPIVA reports show most active managers trail the index over ten-year periods.
rejected.reason: Not verified as in the 2007 book; leave out.

rejected.claim: 'Winners erase the losers' and the 'zero-sum' wording as Bogle's.
rejected.reason: Not verified verbatim; used only the gross-minus-cost arithmetic.

rejected.claim: S&P 500 about 11% a year 1980-2005; missing the best 30 of 9,000 days drops it to 2%; losing 80% of return.
rejected.reason: Not attributed to Bogle in any source found; looks like a generic market-timing statistic.

rejected.claim: Advice list 'stay in, buy monthly, buy more on drops'.
